1.q: רַ֗ב הָיָ֞ה לִ⁠בְנֵ֧י רְאוּבֵ֛ן וְ⁠לִ⁠בְנֵי־גָ֖ד עָצ֣וּם מְאֹ֑ד
1.note: The terms **many** and **very mighty** mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [extremely numerous]

2.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 5:12. This also occurs in verse 25.

3.q: עֲטָר֤וֹת וְ⁠דִיבֹן֙ וְ⁠יַעְזֵ֣ר וְ⁠נִמְרָ֔ה וְ⁠חֶשְׁבּ֖וֹן וְ⁠אֶלְעָלֵ֑ה וּ⁠שְׂבָ֥ם וּ⁠נְב֖וֹ וּ⁠בְעֹֽן
3.note: The words **Ataroth**, **Dibon**, **Jazer**, **Nimrah**, **Heshbon**, **Elealeh**, **Sebam**, **Nebo**, and **Beon** are the names of towns.

4.note: Here, **the face** represents the presence of the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of the congregation of Israel]

The sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are using **struck** as a common expression of the culture to mean “conquered.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [conquered]

The sons of Gad and Reuben are using the possessive form to describe a **land** that is characterized by **livestock**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [{is} a land suitable for livestock]

5.note: See how you translated this expression in 11:15.

The expression **be given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [give this land to your servants]

Even though the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are addressing Moses directly, they are speaking of themselves in the third person as **your servants** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the first person. Alternate translation: [to us, your servants]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **possession**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to possess]

6.q: הַ⁠אַֽחֵי⁠כֶ֗ם יָבֹ֨אוּ֙ לַ⁠מִּלְחָמָ֔ה וְ⁠אַתֶּ֖ם תֵּ֥שְׁבוּ פֹֽה
6.note: Moses is using the question form to rebuke these men. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You must not dwell here while your brothers go to the battle!]

Moses is stating the pronoun **you** twice for emphasis. He is doing this to stress the contrast between these men and their fellow Israelites. If a speaker of your language would use a repeated pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing this emphasis.
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:11. This also occurs in verses 20 and 29.

7.q: וְ⁠לָ֣⁠מָּה תנואו⁠ן אֶת לֵ֖ב בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל מֵֽ⁠עֲבֹר֙
7.note: Moses is using the question form to rebuke these men. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [How wrong it is that you are discouraging the heart of the sons of Israel from passing over]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:2. This also occurs in verses 9, 17, 18, and 28.

8.note: Here Moses is speaking as if the ancestors of these men were their **fathers**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Thus your ancestors did]

9.note: Here Moses is speaking as if the will and courage of the Israelites were their **heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they weakened the resolve of the sons of Israel]
See how you translated this name in 13:23.
See how you translated the similar expression in 23:17. This also occurs in verses 17 and 19.

10.note: Moses is using **the nose of Yahweh burned** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh became very angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 13. Alternate translation: [Yahweh became furious]

By **on that day**, Moses means the time when the spies gave their report to the people, not necessarily a specific 24-hour period. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [when that happened]

11.q: אִם יִרְא֨וּ הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֜ים הָ⁠עֹלִ֣ים מִ⁠מִּצְרַ֗יִם מִ⁠בֶּ֨ן עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ וָ⁠מַ֔עְלָ⁠ה אֵ֚ת הָ⁠אֲדָמָ֔ה
11.note: Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [The men, the ones going up from Egypt, from a son of 20 years and upward, will certainly not see the ground]
See how you translated **from a son of 20 years and upward** in 1:3.

Yahweh is using **they did not fill after me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they were not completely loyal to me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they were not wholeheartedly devoted to me]

12.q: בִּלְתִּ֞י כָּלֵ֤ב בֶּן יְפֻנֶּה֙ הַ⁠קְּנִזִּ֔י וִ⁠יהוֹשֻׁ֖עַ בִּן נ֑וּן
12.note: If it would appear in your language that Yahweh was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [Only Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite and Joshua the son of Nun will see it, because they followed Yahweh completely]

Even though Yahweh is the one speaking, he is referring to himself in the third person as **Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [they filled after me]
See how you translated this name in 11:28. This also occurs in verse 28.

13.q: כָּל הַ⁠דּ֔וֹר הָ⁠עֹשֶׂ֥ה הָ⁠רַ֖ע בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֥י יְהוָֽה
13.note: Moses is not distinguishing this **generation** from another generation that was not **doing the evil in the eyes of Yahweh**. Moses is reminding his listeners that every adult of that generation had done evil. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [all that generation, who had all done what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh]

Moses is using **doing the evil in the eyes of Yahweh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “doing what Yahweh considers to be evil.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones doing what Yahweh considers to be evil]
See how you translated the similar expression in 14:35.

14.note: The phrase **to sweep away** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [to add]

Here Moses is speaking of these men as if they were a **brood** produced by sinful men. He means that they are behaving sinfully as their fathers did. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [men who sin just as your fathers did]

15.note: Moses is using **you will return from after him** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you will stop following Yahweh.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will turn away from following him]

15.q: וְ⁠יָסַ֣ף ע֔וֹד לְ⁠הַנִּיח֖⁠וֹ בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֑ר וְ⁠שִֽׁחַתֶּ֖ם לְ⁠כָל הָ⁠עָ֥ם הַ⁠זֶּֽה
15.note: In this verse, the word **him** is singular in form, but it refers to all the Israelites as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “him.” Alternate translation: [and he will add still to make them rest in the wilderness, and you will destroy all this people]

16.note: The term **pens of a flock** describes enclosures, often built of stone, in which people kept their sheep and goats safe. If your readers would not be familiar with what pens of a flock are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. This also occurs in verse 36. Alternate translation: [walled enclosures]

17.note: The sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are stating the pronoun **we** twice for emphasis. They are doing this to stress that they themselves will fight along with the other Israelites. If a speaker of your language would use a repeated pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing this emphasis.
This could mean: (1) that the people will act quickly. Alternate translation: [as fast as possible] (2) that the people will be ready to fight. Alternate translation: [ready to fight]

The expressions **be equipped** and **being hurried** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [we will arm ourselves and hurry]

The sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are using **from the face of the dwellers of the land** as a common expression of the culture to mean that their children would be “safe from the people who lived in the land.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [protected from the people who live in the land]

19.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [we have already received what we will inherit]
See how you translated the similar expression in 15:23.

The sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are using **toward the sunrise** as a common expression of the culture to mean “toward the east.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [toward the east]

20.q: אִֽם תַּעֲשׂ֖וּ⁠ן אֶת הַ⁠דָּבָ֣ר הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה אִם תֵּחָֽלְצ֛וּ לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה לַ⁠מִּלְחָמָֽה
20.note: Moses is presenting a possible condition: the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben will receive this land only if they arm themselves and fight along with the other Israelites. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Suppose you do what you have said, and suppose you arm yourselves for battle in the presence of Yahweh]

The expression **are equipped** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [if you arm yourselves before Yahweh]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:16. This also occurs in verses 21, 22, 27, 29, and 32.

21.note: Moses is using the adjective **equipped** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. This also occurs in verses 27 and 29. Alternate translation: [every man who is equipped for battle]
The pronouns **he** and **his** refer to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [until Yahweh has driven out the enemies of Yahweh from before him]

22.note: The expression **is subdued** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and you subdue the land in the presence of Yahweh]

Moses is using **you will be innocent from Yahweh and from Israel** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you will have no further obligation to Yahweh or to the rest of the Israelites.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you will have no further obligation to Yahweh or to the rest of the Israelites]

23.note: Moses is speaking of **your sin** as if it were a living thing that could find the person who committed it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that Yahweh will hold you accountable for your sin]

24.note: Moses is using **the thing going out from your mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “what you have promised.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you shall do what you have promised]

25.note: Even though the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are addressing Moses directly, they are speaking of him in the third person as **my master** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [you, sir, are commanding]

26.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 31:9.

28.note: The author is using **the heads of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the leaders of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the chiefs of] or [the leaders of]

30.note: The expression **being equipped** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But if they do not equip themselves for battle and pass over with you]

32.note: The sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben are stating the pronoun **We** twice for emphasis. They are doing this to stress that they themselves will cross the Jordan with the other Israelites. If a speaker of your language would use a repeated pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing this emphasis.
See how you translated these similar phrases in Numbers 32:30.
See how you translated the similar expression in 27:7.

33.note: Here the author is introducing **the half of the tribe of Manasseh** as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and to another group as well, the half of the tribe of Manasseh, who descended from Joseph]

The author is not referring to a specific **Amorite** person. He means the Amorite people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Amorites]

38.note: The phrase **being changed of name** could apply to: (1) just **Nebo** and **Baal Meon**. Alternate translation: [the names of these two towns were changed] (2) some of the previous town names. Alternate translation: [the names of some of these towns were changed] (3) just **Baal Meon**. Alternate translation: [the name of this town was changed]

The expression **being changed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, it could be: (1) Israelites at some later time. Alternate translation: [the Israelites later changed the names] (2) the people of Reuben when they fortified the cities. Alternate translation: [the Reubenites changed their names]

39.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֨לְכ֜וּ בְּנֵ֨י מָכִ֧יר בֶּן מְנַשֶּׁ֛ה גִּלְעָ֖דָ⁠ה וַֽ⁠יִּלְכְּדֻ֑⁠הָ וַ⁠יּ֖וֹרֶשׁ אֶת הָ⁠אֱמֹרִ֥י
39.note: In this verse, the word **he** is singular in form, but it refers to all the descendants of Machir as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “he.” Alternate translation: [And the sons of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead and captured it, and they dispossessed the Amorite]

The author is not referring to a specific **Amorite**. He means the Amorite people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Amorites]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:34. This also occurs in verses 40 and 41.

41.note: The pronoun **their** refers to the Amorites who lived in the region of Gilead. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and captured the villages of the Amorites]
The words **Havvoth Jair** are the name of a group of villages. The name means “the tent villages of Jair.”

42.note: Here the author is speaking as if the villages surrounding Kenath were its **daughters**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Kenath and the villages around it]
